question: Which official body regulates nursing practice and sets the scope for nurses in Nigeria?

options.C: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria
options.D: Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria

explanation: Spot on! The Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN) is our mother body that sets the rules and scope of practice for all nurses in the country.

question: Why are nurses legally responsible for the medications they give to patients, even if a doctor prescribed them?

options.A: Pharmacies lack the legal power to sue clinical staff for mistakes.
options.B: Nurses must share equal financial blame with the hospital owners for drug errors.
options.C: Doctors expect nurses to take full legal blame if a drug reacts poorly.
options.D: Nurses are ultimately responsible for any independent action they take at the bedside.

explanation: You've got this! Even though a doctor writes the prescription, as the nurse at the bedside, you have a duty to double-check that the drug is safe before giving it.

question: What simple inventory rule helps nurses make sure older ward medications are used before they expire?
explanation: Brilliant! The First-In, First-Out (FIFO) rule simply means the drugs that arrived first are the ones used first, preventing waste on the shelf.

question: You walk into the ward and notice the fridge storing insulin was unplugged all night. What is the best step to take?

options.A: Inject a test dose on a stable patient to verify potency.
options.B: Use the insulin immediately before it warms up further.
options.C: Quarantine the insulin and consult pharmacy before using it.
options.D: Discard the insulin quietly without logging the incident.

explanation: Safety first! Heat ruins insulin. Always isolate the suspect drugs and check with the pharmacy team rather than guessing if they are still good.

question: Why are the standard 'rights' of medication administration so important if a legal case of negligence arises?

options.A: They are federal tax requirements for pharmaceutical companies.
options.B: They serve as the accepted standard of care to prove or disprove negligence.
options.C: They guarantee that hospitals will never face patient lawsuits.
options.D: They allow doctors to bypass writing paper prescriptions.

explanation: Exactly! The medication rights represent everyday nursing best practices. Courts look at them to see if standard care was followed.

question: Which of these actions is a dangerous violation of medication safety rules?

options.A: Checking the expiry date on a drug vial prior to preparing the injection
options.B: Signing off that you gave a medication before the patient actually swallows it
options.C: Asking a patient to state their full name before handing them oral tablets
options.D: Verifying a calculated pediatric dose with a senior colleague

explanation: Spot on! Never sign for a drug before it's taken. Documenting care before it happens falsifies records and puts patients at risk.

question: What is the correct way to fix a writing mistake on a paper patient chart?

options.A: Scratch the incorrect word out completely until it is totally unreadable.
options.B: Apply liquid correction fluid over the mistake and write neatly on top.
options.C: Rip the entire page out of the treatment book and start a fresh one.
options.D: Draw a single line through the error, write mistaken entry, and sign it.

explanation: You got it! A single neat line shows transparency. Never use Tipp-Ex or scribble words out completely—hiding mistakes looks like tampering.

question: Why do courts place so much legal weight on a patient's medication chart?

options.A: It determines how much tax the hospital pays to the government.
options.B: It acts as a contemporaneous legal record of the care provided.
options.C: It proves that the pharmaceutical manufacturer produced a safe drug.
options.D: It replaces the need for verbal testimony from the attending nurse.

explanation: Well done! Records written right when things happen ('contemporaneous') are trusted in court because human memory can fade over time.

question: How must controlled medications like morphine be kept safe on a hospital ward?

options.A: Unlocked inside the general treatment room
options.B: In an open plastic tray on the main desk
options.C: Inside the patient's bedside drawer for privacy

explanation: Correct! Controlled drugs are powerful and prone to abuse, so they always live in a secure double-locked space.

question: What is required when you need to throw away a leftover fraction of an injectable narcotic?

options.A: The empty ampoule must be mailed directly to the Ministry of Health.
options.B: The nurse can throw it alone as long as the sink is clean.
options.C: Another licensed nurse must witness and sign the disposal record.
options.D: The patient must sign a waiver confirming the dose was reduced.

explanation: Spot on! Having a second nurse witness and sign waste disposal keeps everyone accountable and prevents drug theft.

question: Which of these is NOT one of the four legal elements needed to prove professional negligence?

options.A: Actual damages suffered by the patient
options.D: Breach of the legal duty of care

explanation: You got it! Hospital bankruptcy is just a financial state—it has nothing to do with the legal checklist needed to prove negligence in court.

question: You accidentally give a patient twice the right dose of their blood pressure medication. What is your very first step?

options.A: Blame the pharmacy assistant for supplying the wrong concentration of tablets.
options.B: Quietly monitor the patient from afar so no one finds out about the mistake.
options.C: Leave the shift early so you are not around when the patient's blood pressure drops.
options.D: Assess the patient's vital signs, notify the doctor, and document the event factually.

explanation: Brave and correct! Patient safety always comes first. Check on your patient, call the doctor immediately, and be honest in your reporting.

question: What legal charge might you face if you force medication on a clear-headed adult patient who says no?
explanation: Exactly! Giving unwanted treatment to a competent adult who refused it counts as battery under the law. Always respect patient autonomy!

question: A lucid adult patient refuses to take their morning drugs. What should you do first?

options.A: Explore the patient's reasons, explain the risks of refusal, and inform the doctor.
options.B: Crush the pills into the patient's breakfast porridge so they swallow them unknowingly.
options.C: Document that the patient is non-compliant and ignore them for the rest of the shift.
options.D: Threaten to discharge the patient immediately if they do not cooperate with care.

explanation: Spot on! Patients have a right to choose. Take time to listen to their worries, educate them on the risks, and keep the medical team in the loop.
